attempts.entry_title: High-degree neurons feed cortical computations (Timme et al. 2016)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's network findings held, on transfer entropy networks rebuilt from the spike times because the paper's networks are not deposited. High-degree neurons were far more common than in random networks, weights spanned orders of magnitude, and a transmitter's out-degree correlated positively with its receivers' synergy in 42 of 49 recordings and time scales. In-degree correlations leaned slightly negative, and the pooled rise of synergy with out-degree did not appear. In the model the degree-modified rule matched the data's correlations most closely but gave the lowest signal-conditioned mutual information of four rules, where the paper reports the highest. The rebuilt significance test passes more chance connections than nominal, and high-degree neurons here are mostly high-rate ones.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Timme et al. (2016) on CRCNS ssc-3, the spike times of 25 recordings of mouse somatosensory cortex slice cultures on a 512-electrode array. It rebuilds the transfer entropy networks at two time scales with the jitter test, and tests the weight and degree distributions, the correlations of synergy with in-degree and out-degree, the information gain, the partial information decomposition examples of Table 1, and the feedforward model.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Timme et al. (2016) from CRCNS ssc-3

outcomes.statement: The analysis used 25 recordings of somatosensory cortex cultures, with 7735 neurons in total after removing neurons with fewer than 100 spikes in the 60 min recording, an average of 309.4 neurons per recording and an average firing rate of 2.10 Hz.
outcomes.source: Materials and Methods, Experimental System, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: only recordings from cortex were used in this analysis (number of recordings: 25 ... neurons with less than 100 spikes in the 60 minute recording (firing rate < 0.028 Hz) were removed from the analysis. Spike sorting yielded spike times for each neuron (7735 total neurons) with a resolution of 50 μs. The average firing rate for each neuron was 2.10 Hz and each recording had an average of 309.4 neurons
outcomes.notes: 25 recordings, 7735 neurons, 309.4 per recording, every neuron with at least 100 spikes, so the deposit already applies the 100-spike threshold. Mean rate 2.103 Hz with spikes over 60 min (reading b), 2.132 Hz over each recording's own length (reading a); both within tolerance. Rates range from 0.028 to 77.5 Hz.
deviations: The rate can be read two ways (criterion), spikes over each recording's length (a, 2.132 Hz) or over 60 min (b, 2.103 Hz); both match, and the measured value is (a), the first reading the criterion lists.

outcomes.statement: The significant TE connection weights, raw and normalized, are roughly log-normally distributed at both time scales and vary over several orders of magnitude.
outcomes.source: Results, Connection Weight and Degree Distributions, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 4A and 4C
outcomes.quote: Similar to these studies, we found a roughly log-normal distribution of significant TE weights ... both TE and normalized TE values varied broadly over several orders of magnitude
outcomes.notes: With ties counted as exceeding and bins t-2 and t-3, the significant TE values span several orders of magnitude: the 99th percentile is 353 to 1160 times the 1st at both time scales, for raw and normalized TE, under both readings. Fits of Eq 21 to the distribution averaged over recordings have R2 of 0.935 and 0.957 (raw TE) and 0.882 and 0.904 (normalized TE) under (f), and 0.939, 0.960, 0.895 and 0.899 under (s); three of eight fall just below the criterion's 0.9, all for normalized TE. With bins t-1 and t-2 every fit has R2 of 0.90 to 0.98 and the criterion holds under both readings; with the strict tie rule the averaged fits have R2 of 0.08 to 0.71. At the stricter threshold (no surrogate at or above the real TE) the fits under (s) have R2 of 0.92 to 0.97 and the criterion holds; under (f) one normalized-TE fit stays at 0.88.
deviations: The TE networks are rebuilt from the deposited spike times; the paper reused the networks of its reference [44] (Timme et al. 2014, PLoS One 9 e115764), which are not deposited. Bins of 1.6 and 3.5 ms, past states the OR of two bins, a 7-bin uniform jitter, 5000 surrogates and fewer than 5 exceeding are taken from [44], Table 1 and Transfer Entropy Analysis, paragraphs 3 and 6, as the paper directs (Methods, Effective Connectivity Detection, paragraphs 1 and 4).

Assumed that a surrogate whose TE equals the real TE counts as exceeding it. [44] takes as the p-value the percentage of surrogates 'larger than' the real TE (Transfer Entropy Analysis, paragraph 6), and M-SIG says 'larger'. Taken literally, a pair whose counts the jitter cannot change ties in every surrogate and is called significant. On circularly shifted trains, where every pair is independent, the strict rule calls 10.8% of pairs significant and the tie-counting rule 0.32%, against the 0.1% of the paper's p < 0.001, so the strict rule is not the test the paper states. The strict rule is run as a variant. Multiplied by the number of pairs, the tie-counting rule's rate gives 8% to 30% of the significant connections of the five tested recordings as expected by chance (pooled 15.8%). No stricter count of the 5000 surrogates reaches 0.1%; the strictest, no surrogate at or above the real TE, gives 0.20% and 13.2%, and is run as the variant 'calibrated'.

Assumed which two bins form the past state. [44]'s text writes bins t-d and t-d-1 (with d = 1, bins t-1 and t-2), while its Table 1 and the paper give a delay window of 1 to 4 bins, which bins t-2 and t-3 give. Bins t-2 and t-3 are used; bins t-1 and t-2 are run as a variant.

For pairs whose jitter moves more than 50 relevant sender spikes, the surrogate counts are drawn from a normal distribution with their exact mean and covariance, not by jittering every spike, to fit the time limit. On DataSet1 and DataSet7 at both time scales the approximation and the full jitter share 83% to 89% of the connections either finds under the tie rule (95.7% to 99.2% under the strict rule), the approximation finding 0.1% to 8.2% more. The number of past states equal to 1 is held at its real value in each surrogate, as [44] states the jitter preserved it.

Sub-networks follow [44], Topology Analysis - Sub-Networks, paragraph 2 (50 random neurons, unconnected ones replaced from the pool, the 75 strongest connections by normalized TE kept; reading (a) of M-SUB), and a group with fewer than 75 significant connections is redrawn, as M-SUB says. Within 5000 draws four recordings give fewer than 500 sub-networks at 1.6 to 6.4 ms (DataSet2 6, DataSet5 0, DataSet10 380, DataSet17 148); these are used as they are. Reading (b), 75 connections at random, is run as a variant.
The fit starts from the moments of the binned distribution; the paper gives no starting values. 100 log-spaced bins span the pooled range of each panel.

outcomes.quote: we found that the information gain remained constant or decreased with added number of inputs ... Both fits produced small negative exponent values, one of which had an error overlapping zero
outcomes.notes: Median information gain against the number of inputs n, fit with A exp(k n). For the normalized gain k is negative at both time scales under (f) and (s) and from n = 1 or 2, and no 95% interval lies above zero: under (f) from n = 2, -0.071 (-0.089 to -0.053) and -0.114 (-0.123 to -0.104); under (s) -0.074 to -0.249. For the gain in bits under (f) k is positive at 1.6 to 6.4 ms (0.008, -0.004 to 0.020, from n = 2), partial by the criterion; with bins t-1 and t-2 it is 0.047 (0.036 to 0.059), which would be not reproduced. The statement's detail that one interval overlaps zero holds only for the gain in bits. 350 to 750 neurons contribute per n under (f), 12 to 750 under (s).
deviations: The TE networks are rebuilt from the deposited spike times; the paper reused the networks of its reference [44] (Timme et al. 2014, PLoS One 9 e115764), which are not deposited. Bins of 1.6 and 3.5 ms, past states the OR of two bins, a 7-bin uniform jitter, 5000 surrogates and fewer than 5 exceeding are taken from [44], Table 1 and Transfer Entropy Analysis, paragraphs 3 and 6, as the paper directs (Methods, Effective Connectivity Detection, paragraphs 1 and 4).

Assumed that a surrogate whose TE equals the real TE counts as exceeding it. [44] takes as the p-value the percentage of surrogates 'larger than' the real TE (Transfer Entropy Analysis, paragraph 6), and M-SIG says 'larger'. Taken literally, a pair whose counts the jitter cannot change ties in every surrogate and is called significant. On circularly shifted trains, where every pair is independent, the strict rule calls 10.8% of pairs significant and the tie-counting rule 0.32%, against the 0.1% of the paper's p < 0.001, so the strict rule is not the test the paper states. The strict rule is run as a variant. Multiplied by the number of pairs, the tie-counting rule's rate gives 8% to 30% of the significant connections of the five tested recordings as expected by chance (pooled 15.8%). No stricter count of the 5000 surrogates reaches 0.1%; the strictest, no surrogate at or above the real TE, gives 0.20% and 13.2%, and is run as the variant 'calibrated'.

Assumed which two bins form the past state. [44]'s text writes bins t-d and t-d-1 (with d = 1, bins t-1 and t-2), while its Table 1 and the paper give a delay window of 1 to 4 bins, which bins t-2 and t-3 give. Bins t-2 and t-3 are used; bins t-1 and t-2 are run as a variant.

For pairs whose jitter moves more than 50 relevant sender spikes, the surrogate counts are drawn from a normal distribution with their exact mean and covariance, not by jittering every spike, to fit the time limit. On DataSet1 and DataSet7 at both time scales the approximation and the full jitter share 83% to 89% of the connections either finds under the tie rule (95.7% to 99.2% under the strict rule), the approximation finding 0.1% to 8.2% more. The number of past states equal to 1 is held at its real value in each surrogate, as [44] states the jitter preserved it.

Sub-networks follow [44], Topology Analysis - Sub-Networks, paragraph 2 (50 random neurons, unconnected ones replaced from the pool, the 75 strongest connections by normalized TE kept; reading (a) of M-SUB), and a group with fewer than 75 significant connections is redrawn, as M-SUB says. Within 5000 draws four recordings give fewer than 500 sub-networks at 1.6 to 6.4 ms (DataSet2 6, DataSet5 0, DataSet10 380, DataSet17 148); these are used as they are. Reading (b), 75 connections at random, is run as a variant.
30 receivers sampled per recording, time scale and reading, where the paper uses every receiver; all combinations of n inputs or 100 sampled ones, as the paper says (Methods, paragraph after Eq 11).
Assumed the gain is normalized by H(I_F) (reading u), as the paper normalizes the PID terms (paragraph after Eq 10); the gain in bits (v) is shown.
The variants (strict rule, bins t-1 and t-2, random sub-network connections, the stricter threshold) use 100 sub-networks per recording and 20 combinations per n, for time.

outcomes.statement: On the example distributions of Table 1, the PID multivariate TE finds synergy only in the synergistic and the synergistic and redundant examples; mutual information misses the hidden self interaction, and interaction information misses simultaneous synergy and redundancy and unique information.
outcomes.source: Materials and Methods, Multivariate Transfer Entropy and Computation, paragraphs 5 and 6; Figure 2 and Table 1
outcomes.quote: Synergy is only found in the Synergistic Interaction example and the Synergistic and Redundant Interaction example
outcomes.notes: Synergy is 1.000 bit in the synergistic and 0.457 bits in the synergistic and redundant example and zero (below 0.001) in the other six. Hidden self interaction, MI(J_P; I_F) = 1 bit with TE and every PID term 0. Synergistic and redundant, II = 0.0001 bits with synergy and redundancy 0.457 bits each. Single and redundant, unique J = 0.750 bits and II = -0.250 bits, equal in size to the redundancy (0.250). The claims file's redundancy form and Eq 8 give the same values on every example.
deviations: Table 1's printed values are typed into the notebook and each column renormalized to sum to 1, as the criterion says.

Synergy is normalized by H(I_F) (paper, paragraph after Eq 10) and uses the claims file's M-PID form of the redundancy. Eq 8 of the version of record takes the minimum over sources once per state of I_F, weighted by p(i_F); that form is run as a variant and gives the same verdicts. The difference is asked of a reader (questions/timme-2016.yaml).

outcomes.statement: The pure Hebbian rule pools connections among the input neurons most correlated with the network-wide signal, the firing-rate-modified rule spreads them to less correlated input neurons, and the degree-modified rule spreads them almost uniformly across the input layer.
outcomes.source: Results, Feedforward Network Model, paragraph 2; Figure 7B
outcomes.quote: As expected, the purely Hebbian rule pooled connections between the most strongly correlated neurons ... The firing rate modified rule spread connections more broadly to input layer neurons less well correlated with the binary network-wide signal. Finally, the degree-modified rule ... spread connectivity almost uniformly across the input layer
outcomes.notes: Fraction of connections from the upper half of the input layer, averaged over 100 models: Hebbian 0.988, firing-rate-modified 0.792, degree-modified 0.505, random 0.502. Ordered as required, with the degree-modified rule within 0.5 +- 0.1.
deviations: The model follows the Methods and Eqs 13 to 24 of the version of record (read from its JATS XML and printed in the notebook). The firing probabilities of Eqs 16 to 19 are turned into the binary signal's current by inverting Eq 13; output current adds I_con = 10 per active connected input. Each rewiring step uses 500 fresh runs; 100 models per type.

outcomes.statement: In a two-layer feedforward model, degree-modified and firing-rate-modified Hebbian rewiring rules qualitatively reproduce the degree and synergy correlations of the real data, the degree-modified rule more closely, while a pure Hebbian rule and random wiring do not.
outcomes.source: Results, Feedforward Network Model, paragraph 3; Figure 7C
outcomes.quote: Both the degree-modified and firing rate modified Hebbian rules qualitatively matched the degree vs. computation correlation results seen in the real data ... The degree-modified rule was closer than the firing rate modified rule ... the purely Hebbian rule and the random network produced correlation results that were qualitatively very different from the real data
outcomes.notes: Real data (s, Pearson): in-degree -0.016 +- 0.117, out-degree 0.127 +- 0.120. Model means (in, out): degree-modified 0.017, 0.114 (match, distance 0.036), firing-rate-modified -0.061, 0.280 (no match, distance 0.160), Hebbian 0.321, 0.022 (no match), random 0.128, -0.009 (no match). The degree rule matches and is the closest, and the Hebbian and random models do not match, but the firing-rate rule does not match, so the criterion holds in part. Under (s, Spearman) the whole criterion holds (distances 0.019 and 0.138); under (f) only the firing-rate rule matches. At the stricter threshold the real data give the same verdicts under (s).
deviations: The model follows the Methods and Eqs 13 to 24 of the version of record (read from its JATS XML and printed in the notebook). The firing probabilities of Eqs 16 to 19 are turned into the binary signal's current by inverting Eq 13; output current adds I_con = 10 per active connected input. Each rewiring step uses 500 fresh runs; 100 models per type.

The model's synergy is the PID of the states of two connected input neurons about the output neuron's state in the same run, without conditioning on a past, which the model's independent runs do not have (the claims file's reading); 2000 fresh runs per model. Models whose output in-degrees are all equal have no in-degree correlation (56 of 100 degree-modified models at N = 20); their means are over the other models, and setting the undefined ones to 0 changes no verdict.
The real data's reference is the mean and standard deviation of the per-recording correlations of the main analysis under (s, Pearson); the other readings and every variant are shown.

Assumed that the degree and synergy analyses use the sub-networks (reading s of M-SUB), as the paper says they were made 'to reduce bias associated with average degree and network size' (Methods, Effective Connectivity Detection, paragraph 5) and the Fig 4 legend matches the random networks' 'sampling statistics to the real data'. Both readings are shown.
Assumed Pearson correlations (reading p of M-CORR), the default correlation of the Matlab the paper used for its fits; Spearman is shown.

Assumed that a surrogate whose TE equals the real TE counts as exceeding it. [44] takes as the p-value the percentage of surrogates 'larger than' the real TE (Transfer Entropy Analysis, paragraph 6), and M-SIG says 'larger'. Taken literally, a pair whose counts the jitter cannot change ties in every surrogate and is called significant. On circularly shifted trains, where every pair is independent, the strict rule calls 10.8% of pairs significant and the tie-counting rule 0.32%, against the 0.1% of the paper's p < 0.001, so the strict rule is not the test the paper states. The strict rule is run as a variant. Multiplied by the number of pairs, the tie-counting rule's rate gives 8% to 30% of the significant connections of the five tested recordings as expected by chance (pooled 15.8%). No stricter count of the 5000 surrogates reaches 0.1%; the strictest, no surrogate at or above the real TE, gives 0.20% and 13.2%, and is run as the variant 'calibrated'.

outcomes.statement: The pure Hebbian rule gives the highest mutual information between connected neurons, but conditioned on the network-wide binary signal the degree-modified rule gives the highest; it alone raises neuron-to-neuron communication while also reinforcing network-wide correlation.
outcomes.source: Results, Feedforward Network Model, paragraph 4; Figure 7D and 7E
outcomes.quote: Unsurprisingly, we found the largest mutual information in the purely Hebbian rule ... when we conditioned the mutual information on the binary network-wide correlation signal, we found that the degree-modified Hebbian rule produced the highest mutual information
outcomes.notes: Mean MI between connected neurons over 100 models: Hebbian 0.090 bits (highest, as the paper says), firing-rate 0.071, degree 0.030, random 0.023. Conditioned on the binary signal: random 0.00230 (highest), Hebbian 0.00168, firing-rate 0.00166, degree 0.00153 (lowest). The degree-modified rule differs from each other rule at FDR-corrected p < 0.001 (Mann-Whitney) but lies below each. The first-order plug-in bias of the conditioned MI, 7.2e-04 bits, is the same for every rule; with it subtracted the order is unchanged.
deviations: The model follows the Methods and Eqs 13 to 24 of the version of record (read from its JATS XML and printed in the notebook). The firing probabilities of Eqs 16 to 19 are turned into the binary signal's current by inverting Eq 13; output current adds I_con = 10 per active connected input. Each rewiring step uses 500 fresh runs; 100 models per type.
MI is estimated from 2000 fresh runs per model, a count the paper does not give (the claims file's reading).

outcomes.statement: With 40 neurons per layer the model gives the same qualitative results, the degree-modified rule again raising neuron-to-neuron communication, though the Hebbian and firing-rate-modified rules give larger conditioned mutual information than in the small model.
outcomes.source: Results, Feedforward Network Model, paragraph 6; S1 Fig
outcomes.quote: As with the smaller model, the larger model produced computation correlation results similar to the results seem in the data for the degree-modified and firing-rate modified Hebbian rewiring rules, but not the pure Hebbian rewiring rule ... As in the smaller model, the degree-modified Hebbian rewiring rule reinforced network-wide activity and increased neuron-to-neuron communication
outcomes.notes: 40 neurons per layer, 320 connections and rewirings, Eq 24 and Eq 23. Connectivity ordering holds (upper-half fractions 0.991, 0.769, 0.502 with alpha and beta recomputed from Eq 15; 0.999, 0.798, 0.501 with them kept). The degree-modified rule's conditioned MI is below the random model's under both readings (0.00094 against 0.00112; 0.00100 against 0.00206); the Hebbian and firing-rate rules' conditioned MI is smaller than in the 20-neuron model (0.00096 and 0.00097, or 0.00147 and 0.00146, against 0.00168 and 0.00166). The correlation match fails under every reading of the main analysis. The criterion fails under every reading, variant and choice of alpha and beta.
deviations: The model follows the Methods and Eqs 13 to 24 of the version of record (read from its JATS XML and printed in the notebook). The firing probabilities of Eqs 16 to 19 are turned into the binary signal's current by inverting Eq 13; output current adds I_con = 10 per active connected input. Each rewiring step uses 500 fresh runs; 100 models per type.

The model's synergy is the PID of the states of two connected input neurons about the output neuron's state in the same run, without conditioning on a past, which the model's independent runs do not have (the claims file's reading); 2000 fresh runs per model. Models whose output in-degrees are all equal have no in-degree correlation (56 of 100 degree-modified models at N = 20); their means are over the other models, and setting the undefined ones to 0 changes no verdict.
The real data's reference is the mean and standard deviation of the per-recording correlations of the main analysis under (s, Pearson); the other readings and every variant are shown.
Both readings of alpha and beta named in the criterion are run (recomputed from Eqs 14 and 15 with N = 40, alpha = 0.0115; kept at 0.023); neither meets the criterion.

findings.statement: The paper analysed the TE networks of its reference [44] (Timme et al. 2014), at time scales 2 and 3 of that study. The networks, the TE values and the sub-networks are not in the data set, which holds spike times only, so the paper's networks cannot be checked; they have to be rebuilt, and a rebuilt network may differ from the paper's.

DataSet19 (2013-01-06-1) lasts 2887498 ms (48 min), where the paper describes 60 minute recordings; the data description says most recordings are 3600000 ms. The first ten recordings (2012) have no spike in their first 8 s.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier tested the TE helper on synthetic Poisson trains and reran some model checks; it gave its own outcome for each claim, and 12 of 14 agree with the record as it then stood.

disagreements.reason: The fit on the average distribution has R2 of 0.08 to 0.61 against the 0.9 required, under both (f) and (s); the spread criterion passes. The low-TE mode (minimum 1.3e-9 bits, fitted sigma of about 3 decades) is very likely spurious connections from problem 1, so this outcome is unreliable.
Passes under (s) at both scales. Under (f) at 3.5 to 14 ms the largest in-degree (480) exceeds the largest out-degree (449). The Wilcoxon test is p <= 0.0015 everywhere.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the revised run, the helper module, the claims file, the README and the attempt record, with the paper. The verifier agreed with all 14 outcomes and found each assumption stated and reasonable. It quoted three places where the text did not match the outputs: the README's run time (now 55 to 65 minutes; this run took 54.6), cell 45's 50 correlations (now 49), and the [44] figures in cells 14 and 16, which it could not check (cell 14 now quotes the passages of [44], Fig 12C and D legends and the paragraph before Fig 3, with its DOI and PMC id). It reported the claims file's M-PID redundancy as a misreading of Eq 8; that question was already in questions/timme-2016.yaml, and the record's deviations now point to that file. Its remaining point, that the tie-counting test is too liberal, is answered with the share of connections expected by chance and a stricter-threshold variant. No outcome changes and none is proposed. Report in transcripts/timme-2016/verifier-2-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: Question for the paper's authors: which bins form the past states of the TE? [44] writes the past as bins t-d and t-d-1 (d = 1), which gives delays of 0 to 2 bins, while its Table 1 and this paper give delay windows of 1.6 to 6.4 ms and 3.5 to 14 ms (1 to 4 bins), which bins t-2 and t-3 give. This attempt used t-2 and t-3 and shows t-1 and t-2; the log-normal fit (Fig 4A, C) and the information gain in bits (Fig 6) differ between them.

Question for the paper's authors: how did the jitter test count a surrogate whose TE equals the real TE? [44] takes the percentage of surrogates 'larger than' the real TE as the p-value. Taken literally, every pair whose counts the jitter cannot change is significant; here that rule calls 10.8% of independent (shifted) pairs significant, against the 0.1% of p < 0.001, and gives networks about 95 times denser than chance, against 20 to 47 times when ties count as exceeding. This attempt counted ties as exceeding.

Question for the paper's authors: were the weight distributions (Fig 4A, C), degree distributions (Fig 4B, D) and the degree and synergy correlations (Fig 5) computed on the 500 sub-networks per recording or on the full networks, and were the correlations Pearson or Spearman? The in-degree correlation (Fig 5A) has a significant negative skew under three of four readings but not under sub-networks with Spearman, and the model comparison (Fig 7C) holds in full only under sub-networks with Spearman. This attempt assumed sub-networks and Pearson.
Question for the paper's authors: Fig 5 gives N data = 40 correlations per panel; with 25 recordings and two time scales there are 50. Which 40 were used?

Question for the paper's authors: how was the synergy of the feedforward model computed, given that its runs are independent and have no past to condition on, and from how many runs were the model's synergy and mutual information estimated?

entries.name: timme-2016
entries.title: High-degree neurons feed cortical computations (Timme et al. 2016)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Timme et al. (2016) on CRCNS ssc-3, the spike times of 25 recordings of mouse somatosensory cortex slice cultures on a 512-electrode array. It rebuilds the transfer entropy networks at two time scales with the jitter test, and tests the weight and degree distributions, the correlations of synergy with in-degree and out-degree, the information gain, the partial information decomposition examples of Table 1, and the feedforward model.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Timme et al. (2016) from CRCNS ssc-3
